title: The Sons of Shah Jahan Fight for the Throne
text:
In September 1657 the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan fell seriously ill in Delhi, and rumors spread that he had died. He had four sons, each governing a part of the empire. His eldest and favorite, Dara Shikoh, a liberal-minded scholar, was at court beside him. In Bengal, Shah Shuja proclaimed himself emperor. In Gujarat, Murad Bakhsh did the same. In the Deccan, Aurangzeb, a seasoned soldier, allied himself with Murad and marched north.

Shah Jahan recovered, but it was too late to stop the war. Aurangzeb and Murad defeated an imperial army in April 1658 and Dara himself at Samugarh in May. Aurangzeb then besieged his father in the Agra fort and cut off its water from the river, forcing him to surrender. Shah Jahan spent his last eight years as a prisoner in the fort, cared for by his daughter Jahanara.

Aurangzeb turned on his ally next. He had Murad arrested at a feast and later executed. Dara was defeated again, betrayed and brought to Delhi in 1659, where he was paraded through the streets on a filthy elephant before being put to death. The French physician Francois Bernier, who was in Delhi, described the crowds weeping. Shuja fled to Arakan and disappeared.

Aurangzeb ruled for nearly fifty years. The pattern did not end with him: his own eldest son, who had briefly gone over to Shuja, spent the rest of his life in prison.
lesson: When a family's inheritance is a prize to be seized, it can destroy the family itself. Clear succession and fairness among children prevent wars that love alone cannot.
people: Aurangzeb, Dara Shikoh, Shah Shuja, Murad Bakhsh, Shah Jahan, Jahanara
source: Francois Bernier, Travels in the Mogul Empire (1670); Jadunath Sarkar, History of Aurangzib, vols. 1 to 2
